rules.statement: A person is tax resident in Spain if any one of three tests is met: more than 183 days in Spain in the calendar year; the main nucleus or base of their activities or economic interests is in Spain; or, rebuttably, their non-separated spouse and dependent minor children habitually reside in Spain.

source.name: AEAT
source.ref: art. 9 LIRPF, Manual de Tributacion de No Residentes cap. 1

rules.notes: PARTIAL: the BOE consolidated LIRPF truncated before the full text of art. 9 could be quoted. Spanish nationals moving to a non-cooperative jurisdiction remain IRPF taxpayers for the year of change and the four following years.

rules.statement: Permanence aggregates three components: certified days of presence, presumed days falling between two certified presences, and sporadic absences, which are ADDED to the count unless tax residence elsewhere is proved by certificate.
rules.notes: THE PART CALCULATORS GET WRONG. 'Sporadic absence' is not a defined trip length; it is an additive concept. There is no de minimis number of days that makes an absence non-sporadic. Do NOT build a rule that treats absences under, say, 30 days as sporadic and longer ones as not. One documented day of presence counts in full whatever the hours.

rules.statement: A double tax treaty tie-breaker overrides the domestic test where the person is resident in both states under domestic law.

source.name: AEAT
source.ref: Manual de Tributacion de No Residentes cap. 1

rules.notes: Norway, Sweden, Germany, the UK and France all have treaties with Spain. Any residency tool must say so rather than returning a bare domestic-law verdict.
